[Bongbong Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos "Bongbong Marcos") began his presidency at noon on June 30, 2022, following his [inauguration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inauguration_of_Bongbong_Marcos "Inauguration of Bongbong Marcos") as the [17th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_Philippines "List of presidents of the Philippines") [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines "President of the Philippines") of the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines"), succeeding [Rodrigo Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_Duterte "Rodrigo Duterte"). His term is expected to expire six years later, on June 30, 2028.

Marcos initially downsized government bureaucracy, especially in the executive branch of the government.[[1]](#cite_note-1) His administration oversaw the post-pandemic return to normalcy with the gradual reopening of the economy, return of face-to-face/physical classes, removal of stringent travel restrictions,[[2]](#cite_note-2) and the lifting of the mask-wearing mandate for outdoor and indoor settings. He also sought to address the rising inflation and shortage of the country's food supply during the beginning of his presidency.

As president, Marcos signed into law the creation of the [Maharlika Investment Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharlika_Investment_Fund "Maharlika Investment Fund"), the first [sovereign wealth fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_wealth_fund "Sovereign wealth fund") of the Philippines.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Under his term, the Philippines ratified the [RCEP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Comprehensive_Economic_Partnership "Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership") in February, and entered into force in June 2023.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) Marcos also went on many foreign trips in hopes to attract more foreign investments in the country. During his term, many Filipinos said they felt unsafe on streets, and the [country's drug problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illegal_drugs_in_the_Philippines "Illegal drugs in the Philippines") has increased.[[6]](#cite_note-6) By the first quarter of 2024, Marcos' performance and trust ratings had dropped significantly, marking an erosion of public trust in him and his administration.[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Tensions in the [South China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea "South China Sea") rose during his administration, with more clashes between the Philippine forces and the Chinese Navy and Coast Guard. The Philippines also virtually lost control of the [Sabina Shoal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabina_Shoal "Sabina Shoal") during his watch.[[9]](#cite_note-The_Manila_Times-9)[[10]](#cite_note-manilatimes.net-10)[*[unreliable source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")*]

As [the son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcos_family "Marcos family") of 10th president [Ferdinand Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos "Ferdinand Marcos") (who was in power from [1965 to 1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Philippines_(1965%E2%80%931986) "History of the Philippines (1965–1986)")), Bongbong Marcos's presidential candidacy has been controversial, receiving criticism from several groups due to [his father's regime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Philippines_(1965%E2%80%931986) "History of the Philippines (1965–1986)")—a period characterized by [violence and oppression against those opposed to his regime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_abuses_of_the_Marcos_dictatorship "Human rights abuses of the Marcos dictatorship"),[[11]](#cite_note-hartfordMcCoy-11)[[12]](#cite_note-kushidaStanford-12) political turmoil, and [widespread corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unexplained_wealth_of_the_Marcos_family "Unexplained wealth of the Marcos family").[[13]](#cite_note-1billion30-13) Some scholars have noted that his campaign was driven by a massive misinformation campaign aimed at [revamping the Marcos brand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_distortion_regarding_Ferdinand_Marcos "Historical distortion regarding Ferdinand Marcos") and smearing his rivals;[[14]](#cite_note-filipinosFallFakeHistory-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) Marcos has stated he won't engage in negative and hateful campaigning and has repeatedly declined joining debates that may lead to such.[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)

In less than two years as president, more Filipinos have become dissatisfied with the administration of Bongb

Economic concerns, rising inflation, joblessness, low wages, and a perceived lack of productivity are some of the emerging factors behind the drop in pro-administration support. The survey also noted that the "Duterte effect" still persists, with opposition parties grappling with the discreditation of the previous administration.[[18]](#cite_note-18) In 2024, Marcos banned [Philippine offshore gaming operators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_offshore_gaming_operator "Philippine offshore gaming operator") that had proliferated under the previous administration, while Vice President [Sara Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sara_Duterte "Sara Duterte") resigned from his cabinet amidst a growing rift in the [Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcos_family "Marcos family") and [Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duterte_family "Duterte family") political families. The year 2025 was marked by the [impeachment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_impeachment_of_Sara_Duterte "First impeachment of Sara Duterte") of vice president Sara Duterte in February 5 by the [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Representatives_of_the_Philippines "House of Representatives of the Philippines") while former president Rodrigo Duterte was [arrested](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrest_of_Rodrigo_Duterte "Arrest of Rodrigo Duterte") in March 11 and handed over to the [International Criminal Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Criminal_Court "International Criminal Court"), leading to the collapse of the Marcos-Duterte alliance; while subsequently the arrest and hand-over of the latter was severely lambasted, as well as massively criticized and condemned by former Duterte administration officials and allies, and by the Duterte's supporters, which led to a [massive protests in support and in solidarity of former president Rodrigo Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demonstrations_in_support_of_Rodrigo_Duterte "Demonstrations in support of Rodrigo Duterte"), and the uncovering of the [massive infrastructure corruption scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood_control_projects_controversy_in_the_Philippines "Flood control projects controversy in the Philippines") that Marcos initially publicized and denounced that have led to a series of [massive demonstrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baha_sa_Luneta "Baha sa Luneta") and [large protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trillion_Peso_March "Trillion Peso March") in condemnation of the ongoing massive corruption scandal.[[19]](#cite_note-VisMin_Protests-19)[[20]](#cite_note-PHProtests-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

## Election, transition, and inauguration

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Presidency_of_Bongbong_Marcos&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Election, transition, and inauguration")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/2022_Provincial_Results_Presidential_Simplified.png/250px-2022_Provincial_Results_Presidential_Simplified.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2022_Provincial_Results_Presidential_Simplified.png)

Marcos earned most votes in 64 out of 81 provinces in the [2022 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Philippine_presidential_election "2022 Philippine presidential election")[[22]](#cite_note-22)


[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Bongbong_Marcos_and_Rodrigo_Duterte_talk_at_the_President%27s_Hall%2C_Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace%2C_6.30.22.png/250px-Bongbong_Marcos_and_Rodrigo_Duterte_talk_at_the_President%27s_Hall%2C_Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace%2C_6.30.22.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bongbong_Marcos_and_Rodrigo_Duterte_talk_at_the_President's_Hall,_Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace,_6.30.22.png)

President-elect Bongbong Marcos (right) and outgoing President [Rodrigo Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_Duterte "Rodrigo Duterte") on June 30, 2022.

Marcos ran for president on a campaign [platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_platform "Party platform") centered on [national unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_unity "National unity") and continuity of [the policies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Rodrigo_Duterte "Presidency of Rodrigo Duterte") of [Rodrigo Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_Duterte "Rodrigo Duterte"), his predecessor.[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24) He won the [2022 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Philippine_presidential_election "2022 Philippine presidential election"), receiving 31,629,783 (58.77%) votes out of a total of 56,097,722, beating his closest rival, [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_(Philippines) "Liberal Party (Philippines)") member and Vice President [Leni Robredo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leni_Robredo "Leni Robredo") by over 15 million votes.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

Marcos became the first candidate in the history of the [Fifth Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fifth_Philippine_Republic "Fifth Philippine Republic") to win by a majority, scoring nearly 59 percent of the vote. His 31,629,783 votes was not only the highest count ever recorded in a presidential election, but close to the sum total of the two previous records combined.

Marcos's presidential transition began on May 25, 2022, when the [Congress of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Philippines "Congress of the Philippines") proclaimed his candidacy as the winner of the [2022 Philippine presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Philippine_presidential_election "2022 Philippine presidential election") held on [May 9, 2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_day "Election day").[[26]](#cite_note-26)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/Bongbong_Marcos_oath_taking_6.30.22_%28PNA%29_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Bongbong_Marcos_oath_taking_6.30.22_%28PNA%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bongbong_Marcos_oath_taking_6.30.22_(PNA)_(cropped).jpg)

Marcos with his family and [Chief Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_Philippines "Chief Justice of the Philippines") [Alexander Gesmundo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gesmundo "Alexander Gesmundo") as he [takes his oath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inauguration_of_Bongbong_Marcos "Inauguration of Bongbong Marcos") as the [17th President of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_Philippines "List of presidents of the Philippines").

Marcos was inaugurated as the [seventeenth president of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_Philippines "List of presidents of the Philippines") on June 30, 2022, at the [National Museum of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Fine_Arts_(Manila) "National Museum of Fine Arts (Manila)"). He was sworn in by [Alexander Gesmundo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Gesmundo "Alexander Gesmundo"), [Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_Philippines "Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines").[[27]](#cite_note-27) The inaugural ceremony was notable for his meeting with outgoing president [Rodrigo Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_Duterte "Rodrigo Duterte") at the [Malacañang Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace "Malacañang Palace") whose departure honors were also held at the complex, the military-civic parade, and his 25-minute speech that gives a view of what his presidency will look like.[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29)

Marcos's leadership style was described by his press secretary [Trixie Cruz-Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trixie_Cruz-Angeles "Trixie Cruz-Angeles") as being "more systematic and efficient", compared to his predecessor [Rodrigo Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_Duterte "Rodrigo Duterte"), who was driven by passion.[[43]](#cite_note-43) Cruz-Angeles described Marcos as "conservative", and "very up to date" with technology and global issues.[[44]](#cite_note-44)

Marcos, in contrast with his predecessor Duterte, is noted for consistently limiting his exposure to journalists and the media. During his presidential campaign, Marcos was criticized for eluding debates and media interviews. After assuming office, he signed his second executive order abolishing the [presidential spokesperson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_spokesperson_(Philippines) "Presidential spokesperson (Philippines)") position and replacing it with a press secretary. Under Marcos, the Malacañang Palace holds fewer press briefings than the Duterte administration, typically holding a single press briefing per week. The Marcos administration also created a "pool" system, in which the [Presidential Communications Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Communications_Office "Presidential Communications Office") limits the number of media members who could attend press briefings or cover certain events.[[45]](#cite_note-45)

Marcos said he would sometimes consult his wife, [Liza Araneta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liza_Araneta_Marcos "Liza Araneta Marcos"), who is a lawyer, regarding "legal matters", saying "I'm not a lawyer, so I need an expert opinion".[[46]](#cite_note-46)

## Administration and cabinet

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Presidency_of_Bongbong_Marcos&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Administration and cabinet")]

Marcos began naming his Cabinet members on May 12, 2022.[[47]](#cite_note-cabinetmembers-47) Following his presidential inauguration, he administered a mass oath-taking of his Cabinet officials.[[48]](#cite_note-48)

Marcos appointed his long time chief-of-staff and spokesperson, [Vic Rodriguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vic_Rodriguez_(lawyer) "Vic Rodriguez (lawyer)") as his [Executive Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Secretary_(Philippines) "Executive Secretary (Philippines)").[[49]](#cite_note-49) Upon the recommendation of his Chief Presidential Legal Counsel, [Juan Ponce Enrile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Ponce_Enrile "Juan Ponce Enrile"), Marcos rejected the plan of Rodriguez to grant himself additional powers as Marcos's new [Presidential Chief of Staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Chief_of_Staff "Presidential Chief of Staff") following his resignation as Executive Secretary on September 17 due to issues involving his roles in [the sugar importation order fiasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Philippine_sugar_crisis "2022 Philippine sugar crisis") and contentious appointments of some government officials.[[50]](#cite_note-DailyTribune-QuitsAsES-50)[[51]](#cite_note-51) He was replaced by former [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_Philippines "Supreme Court of the Philippines") [Chief Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_Philippines "Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines") [Lucas Bersamin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas_Bersamin "Lucas Bersamin") on September 27.[[52]](#cite_note-excjbersamin-52)

On October 4, 2022, Marcos reappointed 10 cabinet members after they were bypassed by the [Commission on Appointments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commission_on_Appointments "Commission on Appointments") (COA) on September 28;[[53]](#cite_note-53) COA chairperson [Jose Calida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Calida "Jose Calida") and Press Secretary [Trixie Cruz-Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trixie_Cruz-Angeles "Trixie Cruz-Angeles") resigned the same day.[[54]](#cite_note-54)[[55]](#cite_note-luminousresign-55)

On May 22, 2025, following the results of [the midterm elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Philippine_general_election "2025 Philippine general election"), Marcos called for the courtesy resignations of his cabinet members, agency heads, and presidential advisers, initiating the first major [cabinet reshuffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Philippine_cabinet_reshuffle "2025 Philippine cabinet reshuffle") since the [Arroyo administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Gloria_Macapagal_Arroyo "Presidency of Gloria Macapagal Arroyo").[[56]](#cite_note-56) Executive Secretary Lucas Bersamin later announced that while the resignations of several officials—including the Secretaries of Foreign Affairs, Environment, and Housing—were accepted and replacements appointed,[[57]](#cite_note-57) others in key economic and security posts were retained.[[58]](#cite_note-58) In a second wave of changes, the Solicitor General and the Chairperson of the Commission on Higher Education were replaced, while the Secretaries of Defense, Justice, and the Interior remained in their positions.[[59]](#cite_note-59)[[60]](#cite_note-60)
